notes:
I've written notes for every verse, but they rest on fewer sources than you asked for. Enduring Word wouldn't open directly (only quoted through Precept Austin), and I didn't reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, newadvent.org or the Lutheran and Pentecostal sites. So there's no modern-scholarship, Orthodox or prosperity/word-of-faith material below. The traditions only really split on v. 2 (Peter as "first"), and a little on v. 1, 5 and 8. Verses 16–21 rest mostly on Spurgeon.

**v. 1**
- Jesus first calls the Twelve, then gives them power. Precept Austin applies this today: whatever He calls you to do, He equips you for. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary
- Broadus says the spirits are called "unclean" because of their own wickedness, and perhaps because their presence defiled the person. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary
- Broadus also traces how slowly Jesus trained the Twelve. At this stage they only go ahead to prepare for His coming, and they still need the Spirit later. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary
- Gotquestions (quoted there): "unclean spirit" is simply another word for a demon. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary
- *Two views on whether this power is for today:*
  - Spurgeon (Baptist) says the Twelve were made to stand for their Lord, and he longs for believers to be able to do what Jesus did. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
  - Henry Morris (conservative evangelical) says the power was given for a special time and purpose, and it is dangerous for others to seek it for themselves (Acts 8:18–20). https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary

**v. 2**
- In every list of the apostles the names come in three groups of four, with Peter always first and Judas always last. https://bible.org/seriespage/matthew-10
- Spurgeon: twelve was a complete number that linked the spiritual Israel with the nation. Peter is "first" because he was the natural, energetic leader. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
- *Traditions differ on "first":*
  - Calvin (Reformed) accepts that Peter was first among the apostles. But he says Rome is foolish to build papal primacy on this verse, because what was true among a few men can't be stretched to cover the whole world. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol31/htm/ix.lxxxiii.htm
  - Gill (Baptist) says "first" doesn't mean Peter had authority over the others. It reflects that he was called first, was first to open the faith to Gentiles, and above all keeps the list in order. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/10-2.htm
  - MacArthur (gty.org) goes further. He says the Greek *protos* means the chief or leader of the group, not just first in a list. https://www.gty.org/blogs/B170724/peter-whats-in-a-name
  - Catholic Answers lists Matt 10:1–2 among its proof texts for the papacy. https://www.catholic.com/tract/scriptural-reference-guide It also argues that Peter stands out in the New Testament more than anyone except Christ. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/simon-the-petros

**vv. 2–4 (the list as a whole)**
- Guzik (Enduring Word, quoted on Precept Austin): the list's main feature is its variety, and none of the men seem to come from privileged backgrounds. Precept Austin adds that no priest, Pharisee or scribe is included. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary

**v. 3**
- Spurgeon thinks Bartholomew is probably Nathanael, who was brought to Jesus by Philip, and that Thaddaeus (Lebbaeus) is probably Jude, "not Iscariot." https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
- He says Matthew calls himself "the tax collector" out of gratitude, so that the grace that called him stands out more. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 4**
- Spurgeon notes the pairing: Simon the Zealot sits alongside the calculating Judas. Judas was probably the group's money-keeper, and that useful gift was twisted into his ruin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
- Ellicott: John calls Judas "son of Simon." Ellicott suggests Judas may have been the only apostle from Judah rather than Galilee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/10-2.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/10.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott admits the limit seems to clash with Jesus' earlier ministry in Samaria. He explains that the disciples had to learn pity for Israel's lost sheep before they could share His longing for "other sheep." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/matthew-10.html
- Benson (Methodist) says the Gentile mission waited until the Spirit was poured out at Pentecost. Preaching to Samaritans now would have put a stumbling block before the Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/10-5.htm
- Gill: going into Samaria wasn't wrong in itself, just not fitting at that time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/10-5.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the Jews deserved to hear first. Had they accepted, they would have become the main evangelists to the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/10-5.htm
- Constable and Barclay: in practice the restriction kept the Twelve inside Galilee. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/10-5.html
- *Is the limit binding today?*
  - Coffman (Churches of Christ) says this commission belonged only to that mission, so its rules don't bind ministers today. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/10-5.html
  - Spurgeon says it allows for special missions to particular groups, but the standing order is "all the world." https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 6**
- Benson: they are called "lost sheep" because they were scattered and leaderless (9:36), and in danger of perishing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/10-5.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes describe the restriction as being about timing, not favouritism. https://biblehub.com/matthew/10-5.htm

**v. 7**
- Spurgeon: their first job was to announce the coming kingdom and prepare the way for the King. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 8**
- Spurgeon: the miracles were to confirm the message. Their powers hadn't been bought, so the miracles weren't to be sold. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
- Calvin: they were not to hold back power given for everyone's good. Matthew Henry: they were sent to do good, not to call down fire. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/10-8.html
- *Textual note:* Clarke points out that "raise the dead" is missing from many manuscripts. He says there's no evidence the disciples raised anyone before Christ's resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/10-8.html
- *Answering that:* "Contending for the Faith" says there's no record of it on this tour, but they did raise the dead later (Acts 9; Acts 20). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/10-8.html
- Bible Hub's study notes point to James 5:14–15 as the church carrying this pattern forward. https://biblehub.com/matthew/10-8.htm
- Kretzmann (Lutheran), quoted in the Light of Israel commentary: removing the miracles takes away the heart of the gospel accounts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/10-8.html

**vv. 9–10**
- Spurgeon: the people would provide food, clothes and even a staff. It is right for those who receive spiritual help to support the minister's material needs. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
- He adds that this method suited a friendly audience, not hostile ground. Luke 22:36 ("take a purse") shows the rules change with circumstances. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 11**
- Spurgeon: choose hosts by their character, not their wealth, and don't go from house to house like beggars. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
- Matthew Henry: their stays were short, and people who keep changing lodgings are rightly suspected. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/10-8.html

**vv. 12–13**
- Spurgeon: the greeting means "Peace be to this house." Think well of everyone until they prove otherwise, and leave the judging of worthiness to the Lord. If the blessing comes back to you, you can take the rejection without losing heart. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 14**
- MacArthur: Jews returning from Gentile lands shook the dust off their feet. Doing this to a Jewish town treated it like a Gentile one. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/matthew-10-commentary
- Ellicott adds the Jewish belief that even the dust of a heathen land defiled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/matthew-10.html
- Spurgeon: do it calmly, not bitterly, but openly, so the act is remembered. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 15**
- Spurgeon: Sodom and Gomorrah's fate will be lighter than that of towns that had the gospel brought to them freely and refused it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 16**
- Spurgeon: the sheep are sent to change the wolves, not fight them. They need to be wise so as not to be harmed, and harmless so as to do no harm. In his phrase, "martyrs, not maniacs." https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon

**vv. 17–18**
- Spurgeon: don't rely on people's approval or tone your message down for them. Jewish hostility would bring in Gentile rulers, and those trials would become chances to testify. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
- Barclay notes that this goes far beyond the Galilee-only mission of v. 5. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/10-5.html

**vv. 19–20**
- Spurgeon: the Father gives the right words in the moment, as martyrs have found. God's servants are His instruments, just as Christ spoke from the Father. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
- A commentator quoted on Precept Austin (the snippet doesn't name him) says this is nothing mechanical or like being possessed. The apostles' minds stay free and aware while they depend on the Spirit. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/matthew-10-commentary

**v. 21**
- Spurgeon: religious bitterness breeds unnatural hatred inside families, and history has shown Jesus' warning wasn't overstated. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-10-commentary-spurgeon
